slides.say: This is about two travelers at once. How fast do they get closer, or farther apart?
Relative speed is the rate at which the gap between two travelers changes.

slides: We don't follow each one on its own. We follow the gap between them.
How many kilometers does the gap change in one hour? That's the relative speed.

slides.say: Now a new example. Mia and Leo stand twenty-four kilometers apart, on the same road.
They walk toward each other. Mia walks three kilometers per hour, and Leo walks five.
Let's see where they are after one hour.
In one hour, Mia walks three kilometers. So she's three kilometers from her start.
Leo walks five kilometers toward her. So he's five kilometers from his start.
Together, they closed three plus five, eight kilometers. So the gap is twenty-four minus eight, sixteen.
Now after two hours. Each of them walks for one more hour.
Mia walks three more kilometers. So she's six kilometers from her start.
Leo walks five more. So he's ten kilometers from his start.
The gap shrinks by eight again. Sixteen minus eight is eight kilometers.
And after three hours? Mia is nine kilometers from her start. Leo is fifteen kilometers from his.
The gap shrinks by eight once more. Eight minus eight is zero. They meet.
Now look only at the gap column. Twenty-four, sixteen, eight, zero.
at: look only at the gap column

slides: Every hour, the gap shrinks by the same eight kilometers.
Why eight? Because every hour, Mia closes three kilometers, and Leo closes five.

slides.say: Three plus five is eight. So the gap shrinks by eight every hour.

slides: So we don't need to find where each of them is. We only follow the gap.

slides.say: Now look at the moment they meet, after three hours.
Mia walked nine kilometers, from her start to the meeting point.
Leo walked fifteen kilometers, from his start to the same point.
Together, their two pieces make the whole road between them. Nine plus fifteen is twenty-four.
So they meet when together they have covered the whole gap.

slides: Every hour, together they cover eight kilometers. They need to cover twenty-four.

slides.say: How many hours is that? Twenty-four divided by eight is three hours.
That's the quick way. The time is the gap divided by the relative speed.
at: The time is the gap divided

slides.say: Here's an easy way to remember that we add.
Imagine a truck that drives at twenty kilometers per hour. A car drives toward it at fifty.
In one hour, the truck covers twenty kilometers, and the car covers fifty.
So together, they close twenty plus fifty, seventy kilometers every hour.
If they crash, it's like a crash at seventy. Toward each other, we add the speeds.
Now a new example, with different numbers.
Sara and Tom start fifty kilometers apart, and ride toward each other.
Sara rides at twelve kilometers per hour, and Tom rides at eight.
They ride toward each other, so we add the speeds. Twelve plus eight is twenty.
So the gap shrinks by twenty kilometers every hour. Let's follow the gap.
At the start, the gap is fifty kilometers.
After one hour, it's fifty minus twenty, thirty.
After two hours, it's thirty minus twenty, ten.
Now only ten kilometers are left. That's less than one hour of riding.
Ten is half of twenty. So they need half an hour more. They meet after two and a half hours.
at: They meet after two and a half

slides.say: The quick way gives the same answer. Fifty divided by twenty is two and a half hours.
Two and a half hours is two hours and thirty minutes.
Let's check that they really meet after two and a half hours.
In two and a half hours, Sara rides twelve times two and a half. That's thirty kilometers.
Tom rides eight times two and a half. That's twenty kilometers.
Thirty plus twenty is fifty. Together they covered the whole gap, so they meet.
Now a new example, with the same Mia and Leo. This time, they start from the same point.
They walk in opposite directions, away from each other.
At the start, the gap between them is zero.
at: the gap between them is zero

slides.say: Mia walks three kilometers per hour, and Leo walks five.
After one hour, Mia is three kilometers from the start, on one side.
Leo is five kilometers from the start, on the other side.
So the gap is three plus five, eight kilometers.
After two hours, Mia is six kilometers from the start, and Leo is ten.
The gap grows by eight again. Eight plus eight is sixteen.
After three hours, Mia is nine kilometers from the start, and Leo is fifteen.
The gap grows by eight once more. Sixteen plus eight is twenty-four.
Look at the gap column again. Zero, eight, sixteen, twenty-four.

slides: Every hour, the gap grows by the same eight kilometers.

slides.say: They walk in opposite directions, so again we add. Three plus five is eight.
Now two quick questions about Mia and Leo.

slides: How far apart are they after five hours? The gap grows by eight every hour.

slides.say: So after five hours, the gap is five times eight, forty kilometers.
And when are they twenty kilometers apart? We need a gap of twenty.
The gap grows by eight every hour. Twenty divided by eight is two and a half hours.
Now a new example. Two cars leave the same town at the same time, in opposite directions.
One drives at forty kilometers per hour, and the other at sixty.
Opposite directions, so we add. Forty plus sixty is a hundred kilometers every hour.
When are they a hundred fifty kilometers apart? The gap grows by a hundred every hour. So a hundred fifty divided by a hundred is one and a half hours.
at: A hundred fifty divided by a hundred

slides.say: So toward each other or apart, we add the speeds. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next part.
